title: $1.3 Trillion Vanished from Chip Stocks in a Single Day. The Fallout Reaches Bengaluru.
excerpt: The worst semiconductor selloff since March 2020 wiped out $300 billion from Nvidia alone. For tens of thousands of Indian-origin employees holding stock in these companies, it is not just paper losses.
body:
The PHLX semiconductor index plunged 10.3 per cent on Friday — its steepest single-day decline since the pandemic crash of March 2020 — erasing roughly $1.3 trillion in market value from the companies that have powered the artificial intelligence boom.

Nvidia, the world’s most valuable chipmaker, fell about 6 per cent, cleaving more than $300 billion from its market capitalisation. Micron Technology tumbled 13 per cent, evaporating $150 billion. Marvell Technology dropped 17 per cent. AMD lost nearly 11 per cent. Broadcom, the company whose earnings report triggered the rout, fell another 7.9 per cent on top of Thursday’s 12 per cent decline, bringing its two-day loss to nearly 20 per cent.

The combined two-session loss for the PHLX index exceeded 12 per cent — numbers not seen since the “Liberation Day” tariff selloff in April 2025.

## What Triggered the Crash

The immediate catalyst was Broadcom’s second-quarter earnings report, released Wednesday evening. The company beat on both revenue and profit, and its AI chip revenue surged more than 143 per cent year-on-year. But it declined to raise its forecast for more than $100 billion in AI chip revenue next year, and its guidance for $16 billion in third-quarter AI chip revenue fell below analyst estimates of $17.2 billion.

“It confuses the market,” said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, noting that investors had expected Broadcom to raise its outlook given the growth trajectory.

A stronger-than-expected US jobs report — 172,000 positions added in May — compounded the damage. The data reduced expectations of near-term interest rate cuts and made a rate hike the base case for the Federal Reserve’s next move, adding pressure on richly valued technology stocks whose valuations depend on low rates.

Two massive capital raises may have also contributed to the selldown. Alphabet’s $85 billion stock offering and SpaceX’s upcoming $75 billion IPO — already two times oversubscribed — are forcing investors to free up capital. “Between Alphabet’s mammoth capital raise, SpaceX next week, and Anthropic likely after that, investors needed to free up capital and they have started to do so,” said Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson.

## Why This Matters for the Indian Diaspora

The semiconductor sector is one of the largest employers of Indian-origin talent in the United States. Nvidia alone has thousands of Indian-origin engineers across its design, software, and research teams. AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and Marvell all have significant Indian workforces. Many of these employees hold substantial portions of their compensation in company stock — restricted stock units, employee stock purchase plans, and vested options that are now worth considerably less than they were 48 hours ago.

For Indian IT services companies — TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Tech — the selloff sends a different signal. These firms derive a growing share of their revenue from semiconductor clients’ digital transformation and AI infrastructure projects. A sudden chill in chip-sector sentiment, even if temporary, could slow the pace of new contract awards and delay project ramp-ups.

The broader market impact also reaches Indian retail investors in the US. NRIs who have built investment portfolios weighted toward technology and AI — a common allocation pattern in the diaspora — are seeing months of gains compress into a single session.

## Perspective Amid the Panic

Despite the violence of the selloff, the PHLX chip index remains up 73 per cent year to date. The AI investment thesis has not been invalidated. What Friday demonstrated is that the gap between explosive growth and market expectations has narrowed to the point where even a strong earnings report that misses on guidance can trigger a correction.

“You’ve had a lot of people here that were just blindly buying the dip,” said Dennis Dick, a proprietary trader at Triple D Trading. “Blindly buying the dip had been winning you money, but that ended today.”

The S&P 500 fell 2.6 per cent on Friday. The Nasdaq was on pace for its worst weekly drop since April 2025 and slipped below its 50-day moving average — a technical signal that often precedes further weakness.

## What Comes Next

Markets will be watching two events closely in the coming week. SpaceX’s IPO, pricing at a $1.75 trillion valuation, will test whether investors still have appetite for high-flying technology bets after a bruising session. And the Federal Reserve’s posture on rates — now that a hike rather than a cut appears more likely — will determine whether the selloff was a one-day repricing or the beginning of a broader rotation away from growth stocks.

For Indian tech workers sitting on unvested RSUs and for NRI investors holding concentrated positions in semiconductor names, the message is the same one that every market correction delivers: the companies may be exceptional, but the prices had been priced that way too.
